title: Consistent Hashing
tagline: The algorithm that lets you add or remove servers from a distributed system without reshuffling all your data.

sections.content:
Imagine you run a caching layer with three servers. Every cached user profile lives on whichever server satisfies `hash(userId) % 3`. Your system is fast, your cache hit rate is 95%, and life is good. Then traffic spikes and you add a fourth server. Suddenly `hash(userId) % 4` produces completely different answers for nearly every key — almost every cached entry is on the **wrong** server. Your cache hit rate craters to near zero. Every request punches through to your database at once. This is the **thundering herd** caused by naive modulo hashing.

**Consistent hashing** is the algorithmic solution that the distributed systems world converged on in the late 1990s, formalised in the landmark 1997 paper by Karger et al. at MIT. Instead of a flat modulo operation, it maps both servers and keys onto a **circular hash ring** — a number line bent into a loop from 0 to 2³²−1. A key is owned by the first server encountered moving clockwise from the key's position on the ring. Adding or removing a server shifts ownership of roughly `1/N` of keys — only the slice between the changed server and its neighbour — leaving all other keys exactly where they were.

This single property — **minimal disruption on topology change** — makes consistent hashing foundational to modern distributed infrastructure. It underpins distributed caches (Twemproxy, Memcached clients), distributed databases (Cassandra's token ring, DynamoDB's partition layer), and load balancers that deliver stateless session affinity. Understanding consistent hashing deeply means understanding how the internet's infrastructure actually routes and stores your data at scale.

sections.title: The Circular Seating Chart
sections.content:
Picture a circular banquet table with seats numbered 0 to 359 degrees. Three chefs are seated at positions 80, 200, and 330. Each guest arrives, finds their assigned seat by some fixed rule ("your seat number is the last two digits of your ticket"), then walks clockwise until they reach a chef — that chef serves them. Chef at 80 serves guests arriving at seats 331 through 80 (the wraparound arc). Chef at 200 serves seats 81 through 200. Chef at 330 serves 201 through 330.

Now a new chef joins at seat 150. Only the guests who were sitting between 81 and 150 switch from the chef at 200 to the new chef at 150. Every other guest at the table keeps the same chef they always had. This is the core insight: a new server only disrupts the guests in its immediate neighbourhood on the ring.

**Virtual nodes** extend the analogy beautifully. Instead of each chef sitting at one seat, each chef reserves **dozens of seats** scattered around the table — Chef A at 45, 120, 240, 310; Chef B at 30, 155, 270, 350; and so on. Now no single chef is responsible for one enormous arc. Their responsibility is carved into many small arcs distributed evenly around the table. Even if one chef leaves, their guests are scattered to many different chefs rather than all piling onto one.

sections.title: The Problem With Naive Modulo Hashing
sections.content:
Before appreciating the solution, it is worth dwelling on why the naive approach fails so catastrophically in distributed systems.

**The naive approach**: given N servers, assign key K to server `hash(K) % N`. This is intuitive, uniform, and fast — a single hash plus a single modulo operation. The distribution is even (assuming a good hash function). For a static N, it works perfectly.

**The catastrophic edge case**: N changes. When you add one server (N goes from 3 to 4), the modulo changes for almost every key. If `hash(K) = 100`, then `100 % 3 = 1` but `100 % 4 = 0` — different server. If `hash(K) = 200`, then `200 % 3 = 2` but `200 % 4 = 0` — same change. Statistically, when N grows from N to N+1, the fraction of keys that change server is approximately `N/(N+1)`. For N=3 going to N=4, that is 75% of all keys. For N=9 going to N=10, it is still 90%.

**The consequence in a cache**: every cache miss is a database hit. If 75% of your keys suddenly point to the wrong server, 75% of your traffic bypasses the cache simultaneously and hammers the database — a self-inflicted denial-of-service attack on your own infrastructure.

**In a database shard**: it is even worse. Data is not merely a cache that can be refilled from an authoritative source. If keys move to different shards, you need to physically migrate data, coordinate reads during migration, and handle partial-migration states. This is an O(N) data migration every time you add a server — operationally nightmarish at scale.

**The root cause**: modulo creates a **global mapping** — a function where every input depends on N. Change N and every output can change. What we need is a **local mapping** — a function where most inputs are unaffected when N changes, and only the inputs near the changed server are rerouted.

sections.title: How the Hash Ring Works: Step by Step
sections.content:
Consistent hashing achieves that locality by exploiting the structure of a circular number line.

**Step 1 — Build the ring**: choose a hash function (MD5, SHA-1, MurmurHash) and define the hash space as 0 to 2³²−1, forming a conceptual circle (the maximum value wraps around to 0). You never store the full ring; you store a sorted array of occupied positions.

**Step 2 — Place servers**: for each server, compute `hash(serverIdentifier)` where the identifier is typically `hostname:port`. The result is the server's position on the ring. Insert that position and the server name into your sorted data structure.

**Step 3 — Route a key**: compute `hash(key)`. Walk clockwise around the ring from that position — in practice, use binary search on the sorted position array to find the first server position `>= hash(key)`. If no server position is found (the key's hash is greater than all server positions), wrap around to the first server — the one with the smallest position on the ring.

**Step 4 — Add a server**: compute its hash position. Insert it into the sorted structure. Only the keys between the new server's position and its clockwise predecessor change servers — they now route to the new server instead of the server that previously followed that predecessor.

**Step 5 — Remove a server**: delete its position from the sorted structure. The keys it was serving are now owned by the next server clockwise — the one that already follows the removed server. Again, only one arc of keys changes hands.

**The key insight on disruption**: each server, if positions were perfectly uniform, would own approximately `1/N` of the ring. Adding a server creates one new arc of size ~`1/(N+1)` that transfers from the predecessor. Removing a server transfers one arc of size ~`1/N` to the successor. All other keys are untouched.

**The binary search detail**: your sorted positions array might have thousands of entries (especially with virtual nodes). Finding the first position `>= target` with a linear scan would be O(total_positions). Binary search does it in O(log total_positions) — fast enough to handle millions of key lookups per second.

sections.title: The Hot-Spot Problem and Virtual Nodes
sections.content:
Basic consistent hashing with one ring position per server has a critical flaw: **position variance**. A hash function distributes positions uniformly at random across the ring. With only three servers, you might get positions at 50, 55, and 200 — giving arcs of size 5, 145, and 210. The server at 200 owns 210/360 ≈ 58% of the key space, while the server at 55 owns only 5/360 ≈ 1.4%. The load is wildly unbalanced.

This is not a theoretical concern. In production with small numbers of servers, you regularly see one server handling three or four times the load of another purely due to unlucky ring placement. This is called a **hot spot**, and it defeats the entire purpose of distributing load.

**Virtual nodes** are the standard solution. Instead of placing each server at one ring position, each server is hashed to **V positions** on the ring, where V is typically 100–200. Each virtual position is generated by hashing a distinct string that includes the server name and an index: `hash('server-A#vnode-0')`, `hash('server-A#vnode-1')`, ..., `hash('server-A#vnode-149')`. All 150 of these positions map to the same physical server; they just spread that server's presence around the ring.

**Why this solves the problem**: with 150 virtual nodes per server, each server participates in 150 arcs distributed across the ring. Even if some arcs are large, others are small — by the law of large numbers, the total arc length for each server converges close to `1/N` of the ring. In practice, with V=150, load imbalance across servers is typically within 2–5% of perfect balance.

**Add/remove with virtual nodes**: when you add a new server with V virtual nodes, those 150 positions are scattered across the ring. Each one takes a small arc from whichever server currently owns that neighbourhood. The migration load is spread across all existing servers, not concentrated on one. Similarly, removing a server distributes its 150 arcs' worth of keys to many different servers — no single server absorbs a disproportionate flood.

**The memory trade-off**: virtual nodes grow the ring data structure. With N servers and V vnodes each, the sorted positions array has N×V entries. At N=100 servers, V=150, that is 15,000 entries — trivial in memory (a few hundred KB) and still fast with binary search. The sweet spot of V=100–200 delivers good balance with negligible overhead.

**Heterogeneous server weights**: virtual nodes elegantly handle servers with different capacities. A server with twice the CPU and memory should handle twice the load. Assign it 2V virtual nodes instead of V. It will naturally own approximately twice the arc length and receive approximately twice the traffic — no special-case logic required.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `_hash` method takes the first 8 hex characters of MD5, giving a 32-bit integer in [0, 2^32). `addServer` places `virtualNodes` entries on the ring, one per hashed vnode key. `getServer` uses a binary search (`lo/hi` with unsigned right-shift `>>>` to avoid sign-bit issues) to find the first position >= the key's hash, then wraps with modulo for the circular behaviour. With 150 vnodes and 4 servers, the distribution check shows each server attracting approximately 25% of traffic — within 1-2% of perfect balance.

sections.title: Replication with Consistent Hashing
sections.content:
Consistent hashing does not just route requests — it also defines a natural, coordination-free **replication strategy** for distributed databases.

**The approach**: for replication factor R, store each key's data on R consecutive distinct servers clockwise from the key's hash position. The first is the **primary** (also called the coordinator); the next R−1 are **replicas**.

**Why this is elegant**: the replication follows naturally from the ring topology. No separate replica placement algorithm is needed. No central coordinator needs to track which replicas exist. Any node that knows the ring topology can independently compute the replica set for any key by walking clockwise from the key's position.

**Cassandra implements this precisely**: its replication factor is configured per keyspace. When you write a row, the coordinator for that row (determined by consistent hashing the partition key) forwards the write to all R replica nodes. A read with `QUORUM` consistency requires ceil(R/2) replicas to agree — automatically balancing availability against consistency. The ring topology makes this decentralised and deterministic.

**Rack and datacenter awareness**: in production, replicas should not all live in the same physical rack or datacenter (a single rack switch failure would lose all copies). Cassandra's `NetworkTopologyStrategy` extends consistent hashing with rack-awareness: when walking clockwise for replicas, skip servers in already-represented racks. You get R replicas across R different racks without any central coordination.

**The N, R, W tradeoff (Dynamo-style)**: Amazon's Dynamo paper (2007) generalised this to arbitrary N (total replicas), R (replicas read from), W (replicas written to). Consistency is achieved when R + W > N. Choosing R=1, W=N gives fast reads, slow writes. Choosing R=N, W=1 gives fast writes, slow reads. R=W=ceil(N/2)+1 gives balanced quorum reads and writes. The consistent hash ring is the substrate — Dynamo overlays its configurable consistency model on top.

sections.title: Real-World Systems That Use Consistent Hashing
sections.content:
Consistent hashing is not just a textbook concept — it is the concrete algorithm inside the infrastructure you use daily.

**Apache Cassandra** uses a token ring that is isomorphic to consistent hashing. Each node is assigned one or more tokens (positions on the ring from −2⁶³ to 2⁶³−1). Data rows are assigned to nodes by hashing the partition key. Cassandra's virtual nodes (`num_tokens` configuration, default 256) are virtual nodes in the consistent hashing sense — each node gets 256 token positions distributed around the ring for balanced load. When you add a node in Cassandra, it takes token ranges from existing nodes automatically — no manual resharding.

**Amazon DynamoDB** uses consistent hashing internally for its partition layer. When a table's throughput exceeds a partition's capacity, DynamoDB splits the partition — a consistent-hashing-like operation that moves half the key range to a new partition while keeping the other half in place.

**Redis Cluster** uses a closely related scheme: 16,384 fixed hash slots. Every key is assigned to a slot via `CRC16(key) % 16384`. Nodes own ranges of slots. Adding a node means migrating specific slot ranges — the disruption is bounded exactly as in consistent hashing. It is a discretised version of the ring: the ring has 16,384 positions instead of 2³², and slot ranges replace arcs.

**Twemproxy (Twitter's nutcracker)**: a Memcached/Redis proxy that uses consistent hashing (with virtual nodes) to shard requests across a pool of cache servers. Used in production at Twitter to scale their caching layer.

**HAProxy and Nginx** support consistent hashing for upstream server selection (`hash $request_uri consistent` in Nginx, `balance uri` with consistent mode in HAProxy). This provides stateless session affinity: the same URL or client IP always goes to the same backend, avoiding the need for a sticky-session database.

**Chord (peer-to-peer DHT)**: the academic Distributed Hash Table protocol Chord (2001) is built directly on consistent hashing. Each peer in the P2P network owns a range of the identifier space (a consistent hash ring of node IDs), stores keys in its range, and maintains a routing table (the "finger table") for efficient O(log N) lookup across the ring. BitTorrent's Kademlia DHT is a variant of the same idea.

**Content delivery networks**: CDN providers route edge cache lookups using consistent hashing so that the same URL hash maps to the same cache server (or small set of servers), maximising cache reuse across requests from different users.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `getReplicaSet` function walks clockwise from the key's start position, collecting physically distinct servers (deduplicated by the `seen` set). Virtual node positions for the same physical server are skipped. With R=3, the function returns [primary, replica1, replica2]. The order is deterministic — every client that knows the ring topology will compute the same replica set for any key, enabling decentralised reads and writes without a central directory.

sections.title: Failure Modes, Edge Cases, and Misconceptions
sections.content:
Consistent hashing is elegant, but production use reveals important nuances that textbook descriptions often skip.

**Misconception: 'Consistent hashing eliminates data migration'**. It minimises migration — from O(total keys) to O(total keys / N) — but does not eliminate it. When you add a cache server, the ~1/N of keys that move to the new server must be loaded from the origin. During this warm-up period, the new server has a cold cache and those requests hit the database. In practice, you add servers gradually and may pre-warm the cache.

**Misconception: 'Virtual nodes are optional'**. For any production system with fewer than 50–100 servers, virtual nodes are mandatory. Without them, hot spots from uneven arc placement are not a theoretical edge case — they are virtually guaranteed to occur in any real cluster.

**Hash function choice matters**: MD5 and SHA-1 are common choices for consistent hashing because their outputs are well-distributed (approximately uniform) across the hash space. Weaker hash functions (polynomial hashes, CRC32 on some inputs) can have clustering biases that cause uneven ring placement even with virtual nodes. MurmurHash3 and xxHash are faster alternatives with good distribution properties, preferred in low-latency paths.

**Thundering herd on node failure**: when a node fails, all its keys route to the next server clockwise. If that server was already at, say, 40% capacity, it suddenly receives 140% of its capacity and may also fail — cascading the failure around the ring. Production systems mitigate this with replica reads (requests spread across multiple nodes), load shedding, and circuit breakers. Cassandra's `hinted handoff` and `read repair` features specifically address consistency during node failures.

**The hotkey problem**: consistent hashing distributes keys evenly, but if one specific key is accessed far more than others (a celebrity's profile, a trending URL), that single key's owning server receives a disproportionate load. Consistent hashing cannot help here — the solution is application-level strategies: local in-process caching, randomised replication to multiple cache slots, or explicit sharding of the hot key.

**Concurrent topology changes**: if two servers are added simultaneously and both operations update the ring concurrently, the sorted positions array must be updated atomically. In practice, distributed systems use a central coordinator (like ZooKeeper in older Kafka, or Cassandra's gossip protocol with a token assignment algorithm) to serialise ring changes and propagate them to all nodes before serving requests.

**The hash ring is eventually consistent**: in a distributed setting, different nodes may have slightly different views of the ring during a topology change (some see the new server, some do not). Requests during this window may transiently route to different servers. Most systems accept this brief inconsistency and handle it at the application layer (cache miss → refetch, database write → replicate to successor).

sections.title: Implementing Consistent Hashing in Practice: Language Patterns
sections.content:
When you implement consistent hashing in a production service, several practical engineering decisions affect correctness and performance.

**Data structure for the ring**: the core data structure is a sorted array of (position, server) pairs. A `TreeMap` (Java), `SortedDict` (Python's `sortedcontainers`), or manually sorted array (JS/Go) all work. The `ceilingKey` operation in Java's `TreeMap` directly gives you the first key >= target, making Java's implementation particularly clean. In Go, `sort.SearchInts` provides the binary search.

**Thread safety**: in a multi-threaded server, the ring is read by every request-handling goroutine/thread but updated only when topology changes. A read-write lock (`sync.RWMutex` in Go, `java.util.concurrent.locks.ReadWriteLock` in Java) lets reads proceed concurrently while holding the write lock only during the brief add/remove operation.

**Snapshot on update**: another pattern is **copy-on-write** — when the topology changes, build a new ring data structure on a background thread, then atomically replace the pointer that request handlers use. This avoids any locking on the hot read path at the cost of memory allocation on each topology change (acceptable since topology changes are rare).

**Consistent hash in a library**: most production teams use a well-tested library rather than rolling their own. In Node.js: `hashring` or `consistent-hashing`. In Go: `github.com/stathat/consistent`. In Python: `uhashring`. In Java: `com.google.code.gossip` or Cassandra's own consistent hash utilities. The algorithm is simple enough that the library is mainly about correctness (proper virtual node hashing) and thread safety.

**Testing distribution quality**: after implementing, validate balance by generating 10,000–100,000 test keys and checking the percentage served by each server. Standard deviation from the ideal `1/N` should be below 5% with V=100. If it is higher, check your hash function's uniformity or increase V.

**Historical context**: consistent hashing was introduced by David Karger, Eric Lehman, Tom Leighton, Rina Panigrahy, Matthew Levine, and Daniel Lewin in the 1997 STOC paper *Consistent Hashing and Random Trees: Distributed Caching Protocols for Relieving Hot Spots on the World Wide Web*. Daniel Lewin, who later co-founded Akamai Technologies (the world's largest CDN), built the first large-scale deployment of consistent hashing for web caching. The algorithm was initially motivated by CDN edge caches — exactly the same use case drives its adoption today in Redis clusters and distributed databases.

**When to use consistent hashing** — and when not to:

**Use it** when: you shard a cache or database across multiple servers that may scale up or down; you need session affinity in a load balancer without server-side sticky state; you build a distributed key-value store with dynamic cluster membership; you design a CDN or P2P DHT.

**Do not use it** when: N is fixed and will never change (simple modulo hashing is faster and simpler); your data access pattern has severe hot keys (consistent hashing cannot redistribute a single key); you need exact, centralised control over data placement (e.g. regulatory requirements to pin data to specific geographic nodes — use a partition map instead); or when you are routing within a single process (just use a thread-pool or channel — network-level hashing adds unnecessary complexity).

**Common pitfall**: consistent hashing solves the *resharding* problem, not the *hot key* problem. If 80% of your traffic hits one key (celebrity effect), you need application-level caching or key splitting — consistent hashing will faithfully route all 80% to the same server.

items: **Naive modulo hashing** (`hash(key) % N`) remaps ~N/(N+1) keys whenever N changes — catastrophic for caches and databases. Consistent hashing bounds remapping to ~1/N of keys by mapping servers and keys to the same circular ring.

**The hash ring** maps all values from 0 to 2^32-1 onto a circle. A key is owned by the first server clockwise from its hash position. Adding a server creates one new arc; removing one merges that arc into the successor — all other keys are untouched.

**Virtual nodes** (V hashed positions per physical server, typically 100-200) solve the hot-spot problem from uneven ring placement. With V=150, each server attracts approximately 1/N of traffic within 2-5% variance, and topology changes spread migration load across all existing servers.

**Replication** follows naturally from the ring: store each key on R consecutive distinct servers clockwise from its position. No central coordinator is needed — any node that knows the ring topology can independently compute the replica set for any key. This is exactly how Cassandra implements its replication factor.

**Real-world deployments**: Cassandra uses a token ring with 256 virtual nodes per server; Redis Cluster uses a discretised 16,384-slot variant; Twemproxy uses consistent hashing for Memcached sharding; Nginx and HAProxy support consistent hash upstreams for session affinity.

**Failure modes to know**: cascading failure when the successor of a failed node is already near capacity; thundering herd during cold-start of a new node; hotkey problems (consistent hashing distributes keys evenly but cannot help a single key that receives extreme traffic); and brief routing inconsistency during ring updates in distributed settings.

**Implementation**: use a sorted array of positions with binary search (O(log V*N) lookup), a read-write lock for thread safety, and validate distribution with 10k+ test keys. In production, prefer a well-tested library (`hashring`, `stathat/consistent`, `uhashring`) over rolling your own.

quiz.question: A cache cluster uses `server = hash(key) % N`. The cluster grows from N=4 to N=5 servers. Approximately what fraction of keys must be remapped?
options: 20% — only the keys assigned to the new server
50% — half the keys change on average
80% — most keys hash to a different server under the new modulus
100% — all keys must be remapped when N changes
quiz.explanation: When N changes from 4 to 5, the fraction of keys that remap is approximately N/(N+1) = 4/5 = 80%. This is because hash(key) % 4 and hash(key) % 5 produce different results for most keys. Consistent hashing limits this to ~1/(N+1) = 20%.

quiz.question: On a consistent hash ring with servers at positions 80, 200, and 330, which server owns the key that hashes to position 250?
options: Server at position 80 — it is the closest server to 250
Server at position 200 — it is the nearest server below 250
Server at position 330 — it is the first server clockwise from 250
Keys are split between servers 200 and 330 proportionally
quiz.explanation: A key is owned by the first server encountered moving clockwise from its hash position. Starting at 250 and moving clockwise, the next server is at 330. Server 200 is counter-clockwise (already passed), so it does not apply.

quiz.question: A consistent hash ring has 5 servers. A 6th server is added. Approximately what fraction of keys are remapped?
options: 1/5 of all keys (the fraction owned by the predecessor)
1/6 of all keys (the new server's fair share)
5/6 of all keys (all but the new server's share)
No keys — adding a server never requires remapping
quiz.explanation: The new server takes over the arc between itself and its predecessor. That arc is approximately 1/(N+1) = 1/6 of the ring. Keys in that arc remapped to the new server; all others are untouched. The predecessor loses 1/6 of its former keys.

quiz.question: Without virtual nodes, a consistent hash ring has 3 servers landing at positions 50, 55, and 200 (out of 360). What is the approximate load on the server at position 200?
options: 33% — consistent hashing guarantees equal load distribution
About 1.4% — it owns only the tiny arc from 55 to 200
About 58% — it owns the large arc from 200 back to 50 (wrapping around)
About 40% — determined by the number of virtual nodes
quiz.explanation: The server at 200 owns keys from just after position 55 (its predecessor) clockwise all the way around to 200 — an arc spanning from 55 to 200 going the long way around through 360/0. That arc covers approximately (360-200+50)/360 * 100 ≈ 58% of the ring. This illustrates why virtual nodes are essential for balanced load.

quiz.question: A server is configured with V=150 virtual nodes in a consistent hash ring. What does adding this server do to the existing servers' key ownership?
options: One randomly chosen existing server loses all its keys to the new server
Each existing server loses a small portion of its keys to the new server, spreading migration evenly
All existing servers lose exactly 1/N of their keys to the new server
No existing server loses any keys — the new server only handles new keys
quiz.explanation: The new server's 150 virtual node positions are scattered across the ring. Each position takes a small arc from whichever existing server previously owned that neighbourhood. The total migration is ~1/(N+1) of all keys, but that migration load is spread across all N existing servers rather than concentrated on one.

quiz.question: In a consistent hash ring with replication factor R=3, where is a key's data stored?
options: On three randomly selected servers chosen anew for each write
On the three servers with the lowest current load
On the R consecutive distinct servers clockwise from the key's ring position
On the primary server and two servers chosen by a central replication coordinator
quiz.explanation: Consistent hashing supports replication by storing each key on R consecutive distinct physical servers clockwise from the key's hash position. The first is the primary; the next R-1 are replicas. This is deterministic — any node can compute the replica set without a central coordinator, which is how Cassandra implements its replication factor.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of looking up the owning server for a key on a consistent hash ring with N servers and V virtual nodes per server?
options: O(1) — the ring is a hash map, so lookup is constant time
O(N) — you must check each server to find the closest one
O(log(N*V)) — binary search on the sorted positions array
O(V) — you walk through each virtual node of each server
quiz.explanation: The ring stores N*V positions in a sorted array. Finding the first position >= the key's hash uses binary search, which runs in O(log(N*V)) time. With N=100 servers and V=150, that is log2(15000) ≈ 14 comparisons — negligible overhead.

quiz.question: Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots. How does this relate to consistent hashing?
options: It is unrelated — Redis Cluster uses a completely different partitioning scheme
It is a discretised consistent hash ring with 16,384 positions instead of 2^32
It is consistent hashing with V=16,384 virtual nodes per server
Redis Cluster uses modulo hashing, which is why it requires downtime to rescale
quiz.explanation: Redis Cluster maps every key to one of 16,384 fixed slots via CRC16(key) % 16384. Nodes own contiguous ranges of slots. Adding a node migrates specific slot ranges from existing nodes — bounded disruption, just like consistent hashing. It is a discretised ring with 16,384 positions instead of a continuous 2^32 space.

quiz.question: A load balancer uses consistent hashing on the client's IP address to select a backend server. A new backend server is added. Which clients are affected?
options: All clients — the hash function changes when a server is added
No clients — consistent hashing guarantees zero disruption
Only the ~1/N fraction of clients whose IP hashes fall in the new server's arc
Clients are reassigned randomly; roughly half will get a different backend
quiz.explanation: The new server takes over the ring arc from its predecessor. Only clients whose IP hashes fall in that arc (~1/N of clients) are routed to the new server. All other clients continue to reach the same backend they always did — their cached sessions and warm application state are preserved.

quiz.question: Which failure scenario does consistent hashing NOT protect against?
options: A single server failing and its keys routing to the successor
A server being added and remapping most of the key space
A single extremely hot key receiving 80% of all cache traffic
Uneven load distribution due to unlucky random server placement
quiz.explanation: Consistent hashing distributes keys evenly across servers, but it cannot help when one specific key receives extreme traffic (the 'hot key' or 'celebrity effect'). Every request for that key routes to the same server — consistent hashing faithfully, correctly puts it there every time. Solutions require application-level techniques: local in-process caching, key splitting (fan out the hot key to multiple cache entries), or rate limiting.
